subject: Science
question_short_text: Identify the experiment employing three spacecraft in an equilateral triangle formation with lasers
text: "The experiment will employ a trio of spacecraft flying in formation in the shape of an equilateral triangle that has sides one million kilometres long, with lasers shining between the craft." The experiment in question refers to:
explanation: Evolved LISA (eLISA) is the proposed space mission designed to detect gravitational waves using three spacecraft in a triangular formation with laser interferometry. The question's description of an equilateral triangle with sides one million kilometres long—actually 2.5 million km in the refined design—matches LISA's constellation architecture.

research.summary:
The question tests recognition of LISA's distinctive mission architecture. Evolved LISA (eLISA), now officially called LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna), is a joint ESA-NASA mission designed as the first space-based gravitational wave observatory. The core concept involves three identical spacecraft separated by 2.5 million kilometres flying in an equilateral triangle formation, with laser beams continuously exchanged between them to detect minute changes in distance caused by passing gravitational waves.

The trap lies in confusing this with the other options: Voyager-2 and New Horizons are deep-space probes studying planets and the Kuiper Belt respectively—they are single spacecraft with no formation flying or laser interferometry architecture. LISA Pathfinder, by contrast, was a precursor mission (launched 2015, ended 2017) that tested the technology on a much smaller scale—two test masses separated by only 38 centimetres inside a single spacecraft, not three separate spacecraft millions of kilometres apart.

Evolved LISA represents the scaled-up, full gravitational wave detection version. The reduced design initially studied had two 1-million-kilometre arms (hence the "one million kilometres" in the question stem), but the final adopted mission (formally approved by ESA in January 2024) uses the full-scale three spacecraft, 2.5-million-kilometre separation architecture. LISA is expected to launch in 2035, enabling detection of lower-frequency gravitational waves from sources like supermassive black hole mergers that ground-based detectors like LIGO cannot observe due to seismic and thermal noise limitations.
facts: LISA Pathfinder (2015–2017) was a single-spacecraft proof-of-concept that tested free-falling test masses over 38 cm; its success paved the way for the full LISA mission.

LISA's three spacecraft will orbit the Sun approximately 50 million kilometres behind Earth, maintaining a triangular formation where laser interferometry measures distance changes to picometer precision.

Ground-based detectors like LIGO are limited to frequencies around 100 hertz and above; space-based LISA can detect lower frequencies (1 hertz or below), making it sensitive to supermassive black hole mergers and other exotic events.
Evolved LISA was originally proposed as a reduced-cost design during ESA budget constraints; the full LISA mission was later formally adopted by ESA in 2024 with construction beginning in 2025.

LISA's inter-spacecraft laser beams must detect distance changes smaller than a nanometre (caused by gravitational waves), requiring technology nearly 100,000 times more sensitive than conventional drag-free satellite systems.
